---
title: "Connecting RStudio to GitHub"
subtitle: "Guide 2 of 4 · do this once"
---

This is the step that fails most often, and always for one of two reasons: Git
does not know who you are, or GitHub will not accept your password. Both are
fixed below, permanently, in about ten minutes.

Work through the five steps in order. Everything goes in the RStudio
**Console** (the pane where R runs), not the Terminal.

## 1. Create a GitHub account

Sign up at [github.com/signup](https://github.com/signup). Two pieces of advice
you will be glad of later:

- **Choose a username you would put on a CV.** It becomes part of every URL you
  share, it is public, and changing it later breaks your links. Something close
  to your real name works well.
- **Use an email address you will keep.** If you sign up with a school address,
  add a personal one as a secondary email under **Settings > Emails** before you
  graduate, so you do not lose the account when the school address is closed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## In this course

Sign up with your NYU address so the roster can match your account to your
NetID. You will also be invited to the course GitHub organization by email:
accept that invitation before anything else, because the assignment links do
not work until you are a member. Invitations expire after seven days.
:::

## 2. Tell Git who you are

Git stamps every commit with a name and an email. It refuses to commit until you
supply them.

```r
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))   # if you have not already

usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "you@example.edu"
)
```

Use the email address attached to your GitHub account. If the two do not match,
your commits will still work but GitHub will not credit them to your profile.

The name is a display name, not a login, so write it the way you would sign an
email. A username with no spaces works too.

## 3. Create a personal access token

GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations in 2021. When
RStudio asks you to push and you type your GitHub password, it will be rejected
every time. You need a **personal access token** (PAT) instead: a long random
string that acts as a password for Git alone, and that you can revoke without
touching your account.

```r
usethis::create_github_token()
```

This opens GitHub in your browser with the right permissions already ticked. On
that page:

1. Replace the placeholder **Note** (`DESCRIBE THE TOKEN'S USE CASE`) with
   something you will recognize later, such as `RStudio on my laptop`.
2. Set the **Expiration**. The default is 30 days, which is almost never what
   you want: your pushes will silently start failing a month from now. Open the
   dropdown, choose **Custom**, and pick a date at the end of your project or
   term.
3. Leave the checked scopes alone. `usethis` has already selected **repo**,
   **user**, **gist**, and **workflow**, which is what RStudio needs.
4. Scroll down and click **Generate token**.

::: {.callout-important}
## Copy the token now

The token is shown exactly once. Copy it before you leave the page. If you lose
it, nothing is broken, you just generate a new one and start this step again.

Treat it like a password: never paste it into a script, a `.qmd` file, or a
chat message, and never commit it. If it ever leaks, delete it under
**Settings > Developer settings > Personal access tokens** and make a new one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## In this course

Set the expiration to **December 31, 2026**, which covers the whole semester
with room to spare. A 30-day default token expires in the middle of October,
which is exactly when you do not want to be debugging authentication.
:::

## 4. Store the token

Back in the RStudio Console:

```r
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Paste the token when prompted and press Enter. It goes into your operating
system's credential store (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on Windows), so
you do this once per computer, not once per project.

If a token is already stored, `gitcreds_set()` shows you a short menu; choose
the option to **replace** it.

## 5. Check the whole setup

```r
usethis::git_sitrep()
```

This prints a situation report. These are the lines that matter:

```
Git config (global)
* Name: 'Your Name'
* Email: 'you@example.edu'
...
GitHub
* Default GitHub host: 'https://github.com'
* Personal access token for 'https://github.com': '<discovered>'
* GitHub user: 'yourusername'
* Token scopes: 'gist, repo, user, workflow'
```

Name and email filled in, a token **discovered**, and a GitHub username shown
means you are connected. If the token line says `<unset>`, step 4 did not take
effect: run `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()` again.

Do not worry about the other lines. `Vaccinated: FALSE` and an unset global
gitignore are suggestions, not problems, and nothing on this page depends on
them.

## When your token expires

Tokens are supposed to expire. When yours does, pushes start failing with an
authentication error even though nothing about your setup changed. GitHub emails
you a warning a week beforehand.

The fix is steps 3 and 4 again:

```r
usethis::create_github_token()   # generate a fresh one
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()         # choose "replace" and paste it
```

You do not need to touch your repositories, and no work is lost.

## A note on SSH keys

There is a second way to authenticate, using an SSH key pair instead of a token.
It is a little more setup once and a little less maintenance afterward, and it
is a perfectly good choice if you already have keys.

Tokens are recommended here because they work identically on every operating
system, they are what `usethis` automates, and expiry makes them safer on a
shared or borrowed machine. If you want SSH, `usethis::use_git_protocol("ssh")`
and the [Happy Git with R](https://happygitwithr.com/ssh-keys) chapter cover it.
